items.followUp: Name two accessory pigments and state how they help in photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Award for identifying accessory pigments.
rubric.description: Names accessory pigments such as chlorophyll b and carotenoids.
rubric.how: Accept either a correct pigment name or group of pigments.

rubric.why: Accessory pigments broaden the range of light absorbed for photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Explains that accessory pigments absorb light and transfer its energy to chlorophyll a.
rubric.how: Require the idea of light absorption and energy transfer to chlorophyll a.

modelAnswer: Accessory pigments include chlorophyll b and carotenoids, such as carotenes and xanthophylls.
They absorb light wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a for photosynthesis.

items.followUp: Explain how the shape of an enzyme’s active site relates to its substrate.

rubric.why: The model explains enzyme specificity through the matching shapes of enzyme and substrate.
rubric.description: States that the active site has a shape specific to its substrate, which fits into it.
rubric.how: Require a clear shape-matching or specific-fit idea.

rubric.why: The lock-and-key model describes complex formation followed by product release without changing the enzyme.
rubric.description: Mentions formation of an enzyme-substrate complex and release of products, with the enzyme unchanged.
rubric.how: Accept either a correct account of the complex and product release or the enzyme remaining unchanged after the reaction.

modelAnswer: The enzyme’s active site has a specific shape that matches its substrate, just as a key fits a particular lock.
The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.

items.followUp: What is a coenzyme, and how does it help an enzyme?

rubric.why: A cofactor is distinguished from the protein part of an enzyme by being non-protein.
rubric.description: Defines a cofactor as a non-protein component of an enzyme.
rubric.how: Require that the component is described as non-protein.

rubric.why: The cofactor is needed for the enzyme to function properly.
rubric.description: States that the cofactor is required for or assists enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Require a link between the cofactor and enzyme function.

modelAnswer: A cofactor is a non-protein component required by some enzymes.
It helps the enzyme function or become active.

items.followUp: State one difference between soluble and insoluble dietary fibre.

rubric.why: Solubility in water is the defining difference for soluble fibre.
rubric.description: States that soluble dietary fibre dissolves in water.
rubric.how: Require an explicit statement that soluble fibre dissolves in water.

rubric.why: Insoluble fibre is distinguished by not dissolving in water.
rubric.description: States that insoluble dietary fibre does not dissolve in water.
rubric.how: Require an explicit statement that insoluble fibre does not dissolve in water.

modelAnswer: Soluble dietary fibre dissolves in water and can form a gel.
Insoluble dietary fibre does not dissolve in water; it adds bulk to faeces and helps bowel movement.

items.followUp: How is pulse rate related to the heartbeat?

rubric.why: A heartbeat is one cycle of the heart’s rhythmic activity.
rubric.description: Defines heartbeat as the rhythmic contraction and relaxation of the heart.
rubric.how: Require both the heart’s rhythmic action and contraction/relaxation.

rubric.why: Pulse rate is expressed as the number of arterial pulses in a unit of time.
rubric.description: Defines pulse rate as the number of pulses felt in the arteries per minute.
rubric.how: Require pulses counted per minute; the arterial location may be stated.

modelAnswer: A heartbeat is one rhythmic cycle of contraction and relaxation of the heart.
Pulse rate is the number of pulses in the arteries per minute, produced by the heartbeats.

items.followUp: Describe what happens to the diaphragm, ribs and air pressure during inhalation and exhalation.

rubric.why: These muscle movements bring about inspiration.
rubric.description: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens, while the ribs move up and out.
rubric.how: Require the diaphragm movement and the rib movement.

rubric.why: Expansion of the chest lowers the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Connects increased thoracic volume with decreased pressure and air entering the lungs.
rubric.how: Require the volume-pressure relationship and inward airflow.

rubric.why: These movements bring about expiration.
rubric.description: During exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped, while the ribs move down and in.
rubric.how: Require the diaphragm movement and the rib movement.

rubric.why: A decrease in chest volume raises lung pressure and drives air out.
rubric.description: Connects decreased thoracic volume with increased pressure and air leaving the lungs.
rubric.how: Require the volume-pressure relationship and outward airflow.

modelAnswer: Inhalation (inspiration): the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs up and out.
The thoracic cavity expands; lung pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air enters the lungs.
Exhalation (expiration): the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped, and the ribs move down and in as the intercostal muscles relax.
The thoracic cavity becomes smaller; lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, so air is forced out.

items.followUp: Name the cell types in xylem and phloem, and state the function of each tissue.

rubric.why: Compound tissues consist of different kinds of cells working together.
rubric.description: Defines compound tissue as a tissue made of different cell types that work together.
rubric.how: Require both multiple cell types and their cooperation.

rubric.why: These are the principal components of xylem.
rubric.description: Names the xylem components: vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
rubric.how: Award for naming the main xylem components; accept the spelling variation “fibers”.

rubric.why: Xylem conducts water and minerals through the plant and also supports it.
rubric.description: States that xylem transports water and mineral salts from roots towards leaves; it also provides support.
rubric.how: Require the transport function and direction or source and destination.

rubric.why: These are the principal components of phloem.
rubric.description: Names the phloem components: sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
rubric.how: Award for naming the main phloem components; accept the spelling variation “fibers”.

rubric.why: Phloem transports organic food made in leaves to other parts of the plant.
rubric.description: States that phloem translocates food from leaves to other parts of the plant.
rubric.how: Require food transport and identify the leaves as its source or other plant parts as destinations.

modelAnswer: Compound tissues consist of different types of cells that work together to perform a common function.
Xylem is made up of vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
Xylem carries water and mineral salts from the roots towards the leaves and also provides support.
Phloem is made up of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
Phloem transports (translocates) food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.followUp: Describe how bile helps in the digestion of fats and name one other important function of the liver.

rubric.why: The question asks whether the liver is a vital organ as well as how it assists digestion.
rubric.description: Identifies the liver as a vital organ and/or states that it performs essential metabolic functions.
rubric.how: Require an explicit statement that the liver is vital or essential.

rubric.why: Bile is the liver’s main digestive secretion.
rubric.description: States that the liver produces or secretes bile.
rubric.how: Require the liver to be identified as the source of bile.

rubric.why: Bile salts break large fat globules into smaller droplets, aiding fat digestion.
rubric.description: Explains that bile emulsifies fats into small droplets.
rubric.how: Require the idea of emulsification or breaking fat into smaller droplets.

rubric.why: Emulsification helps digestive enzymes act on fats; bile also helps neutralise acidic chyme.
rubric.description: Explains how bile aids digestion, such as by increasing the surface area for lipase or helping neutralise acidic chyme.
rubric.how: Require one correct explanation of the benefit of bile in digestion.

modelAnswer: The liver is a vital organ and the largest gland of the body; it performs essential functions, including processing nutrients and detoxifying harmful substances.
It produces bile, which is stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine.
Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into tiny droplets; bile is not an enzyme.
This increases the surface area for lipase to digest fats, and the alkaline bile also helps neutralise acidic chyme from the stomach.
